scenarios.title: Harbourside Dental Practice
scenarios.stem:
Harbourside Dental Practice in Plymouth has four dentists and two receptionists.

Patients currently book appointments by telephone. Receptionists write each appointment in a paper diary and keep patient records in filing cabinets.

The practice manager wants patients to book appointments online and plans to store all patient records, including X-ray images, on a new computer system.

scenarios.title: Northway Bikes
scenarios.stem:
Northway Bikes rents bicycles to the public in Newcastle. Customers use a mobile app to find a bike at one of 40 docking stations, unlock it by scanning a QR code, and pay when they return it.

The head office has 25 staff who manage the app, bookings and customer support.

scenarios.title: Castle Lane Primary School
scenarios.stem:
Castle Lane Primary School has 210 pupils aged 4 to 11. Teachers use laptops, and the school is buying 30 tablets for pupils to use in lessons.

An IT technician visits one day a week to maintain the school’s computer system.

scenarios.title: Greenleaf Architects
scenarios.stem:
Greenleaf Architects designs houses in Bristol. The firm has an office with three rooms.

**Design studio:** six desktop computers and one large-format printer.

**Meeting room:** a smart TV that staff and visitors cast presentations to without cables.

**Server cupboard:** a file server that stores all drawings, and the connection to the internet.

**Site visits:** architects take a tablet to building sites and need to open drawings stored on the file server.

scenarios.title: Maple Leaf Care Homes
scenarios.stem:
Maple Leaf runs four care homes in Yorkshire. Carers currently record residents’ care notes on paper at the end of each shift.

The company plans to use an online care-management system. Carers will record notes on handheld devices while they work, and managers will be able to see the notes from any of the four homes.

scenarios.title: Trent Valley Building Society
scenarios.stem:
Trent Valley Building Society has 12 branches in the Midlands. Members can manage their savings accounts through a website and a mobile app.

Branch staff can view and update members’ personal and financial details.

scenarios.title: Brightside Events
scenarios.stem:
Brightside Events runs a three-day music festival for 20,000 people each summer.

All tickets are sold through Brightside’s website. Customers create an account and receive an e-ticket with a QR code.

scenarios.title: Coastline Logistics
scenarios.stem:
Coastline Logistics delivers parcels for online shops from a warehouse in Felixstowe. It has 60 delivery vans.

Staff record stock arriving at the warehouse using handheld barcode scanners.

scenarios.title: Hotel online booking
scenarios.stem:
A hotel in England takes accommodation reservations and restaurant bookings over the telephone and enters the details in a paper diary.

The owners are considering using an online booking system.

The information from the online booking form will be stored on a new computer system that will be set up in the office.

scenarios.title: Travel agency
scenarios.stem:
A travel agency has its main office in Carlisle with several branches around the UK.

Suitable application software has been installed on the travel agency's computer system so that staff can perform their day-to-day tasks.

scenarios.title: James, financial adviser
scenarios.stem:
James is a financial adviser and works for a company based in Leicester. James often works remotely when visiting clients to discuss financial plans.

When James visits clients he uses a laptop with suitable software to capture data and information about the client and their financial plans.

At the end of each visit, James creates a personal area network (PAN) between his laptop and his smartphone to connect to the company server.

**The company has an office with three rooms.**

Server room
A central server that stores all the financial data and information

Manager's office
One desktop computer
One printer

Main office
Four desktop computers for staff to use when working in the office
One Printer

**Client visits**

James' equipment
A laptop
A smartphone

scenarios.title: Just U Games
scenarios.stem:
Just U Games is an online gaming platform.

Just U Games currently stores all the data it collects on a file server on site.

Just U Games is considering how it can use cloud computing to backup this data.

scenarios.title: Riverside Veterinary Clinic
scenarios.stem:
Riverside Veterinary Clinic in Norwich has three vets, four nurses and two receptionists.

Vets write consultation notes on paper and type them up at the end of the day. The clinic plans to give each vet a tablet to record notes during consultations.

One of the receptionists, Priya, is partially sighted.

The clinic is also choosing new practice-management software to store pet and owner records.

scenarios.title: Swift Parcels depot
scenarios.stem:
Swift Parcels runs a delivery depot in Doncaster.

Office staff use desktop computers. Warehouse staff use handheld scanners to log parcels as they arrive. Drivers use smartphones to record each delivery.

The depot is replacing its old network.

scenarios.title: Harmony Music School
scenarios.stem:
Harmony Music School in Bristol teaches lessons in its building and streams live lessons to students at home.

**The school has two rooms.**

Studio
One desktop computer
One webcam
One microphone

Office
Two desktop computers
One printer
One server that stores recorded lessons

**Remote lessons**

Each teacher has a laptop to teach from home.
Students join lessons on their own devices over their home broadband.

scenarios.title: Paws Rescue
scenarios.stem:
Paws Rescue is an animal-welfare charity with 200 volunteers across the North West.

Volunteers organise themselves by email. The charity wants an online community where volunteers can share news, arrange shifts and post photos of animals waiting for adoption.

The charity has a small budget and one part-time IT volunteer.

scenarios.title: FitZone gyms
scenarios.stem:
FitZone runs six gyms in the West Midlands.

It is launching a member app. Members will use it to book classes, pay for sessions and watch exercise videos.

The app will record what each member books and buys. FitZone wants to use this data to send members personalised offers.

Each gym has a reception computer that runs the booking system.

scenarios.title: Bell & Okafor Architects
scenarios.stem:
Bell & Okafor Architects is a practice of 15 architects in Leeds.

Architects create large, detailed building drawings and send them to clients and builders by email and file-sharing links. They often work on building sites, using the site's public Wi-Fi.

The practice is moving to a new office and is choosing new IT systems.

scenarios.title: CareWell Home Support
scenarios.stem:
CareWell Home Support sends carers to visit elderly clients in their own homes across rural Shropshire.

**The agency has an office with two rooms.**

Server room
One server that stores every client's care plan

Main office
Three desktop computers for office staff
One printer

**Carers**

Each carer has a smartphone to view care plans and record each visit.
Some office staff also work from home on laptops.

scenarios.title: Ashford Town Library
scenarios.stem:
Ashford Town Library lends books and offers free public computers.

The library records every book a member borrows and logs which websites are visited on its public computers.

The council is considering new technology for the library, including AI tools and faster networking.

scenarios.title: Crumbs & Co bakeries
scenarios.stem:
Crumbs & Co has eight bakeries in Kent.

Each shop has two EPOS tills that record every sale and update stock levels.

Customers will soon be able to order cakes online and collect them in store.

The tills and the online shop store customers' names, phone numbers and payment details.

scenarios.title: Northlight Films
scenarios.stem:
Northlight Films is a small production company in Manchester.

Editors work in an editing suite at the office. Camera crews film on location, and raw footage files are very large.

Directors often watch edits remotely over a live video link and give feedback as the editor works.

scenarios.title: Keystone Estates
scenarios.stem:
Keystone Estates is an estate agent with two branches.

**Exeter branch**
Three desktop computers
One printer
One server that stores property listings and photos

**Plymouth branch**
Two desktop computers
One printer

**Agents**
Each agent has a tablet to photograph properties and upload listings while out on valuations.

The company website shows every property with its photos.

scenarios.title: ArenaPlay Esports
scenarios.stem:
ArenaPlay runs esports tournaments in hired venues across the UK.

Up to 200 players compete on the venue's network while matches are streamed live online.

ArenaPlay is replacing its spreadsheets and email with a new online booking and tournament-management system.

questions.context: The practice will buy new hardware for the reception desk and the treatment rooms.
questions.question: Give **two** input devices, other than a keyboard and a mouse, the practice could use to capture patient information.
traps: "other than a keyboard and a mouse": the two most obvious answers score nothing here.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: Touch screen / tablet (e.g. patient check-in)
Scanner / document scanner (e.g. scanning old paper records)
Camera / webcam (e.g. patient photo)
Signature pad / stylus (e.g. consent forms)
Card reader (e.g. payment)
Microphone (e.g. voice notes)
Digital X-ray sensor
accept: Any other input device that fits a dental practice
reject: Keyboard or mouse (excluded by the question)
Output devices such as a printer or monitor

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Scanner
2. Touch screen

questions.question: Give **two** characteristics of storage media the practice should consider when choosing where to store the X-ray images.
traps: It asks for characteristics (capacity, speed, cost…), not for storage devices. Naming "SSD" or "USB stick" scores nothing.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: Capacity (X-ray images are large files)
Speed / read-write / access time
Cost (per GB)
Reliability / durability / lifespan
Portability
Security (e.g. supports encryption)
reject: Brand names or device types on their own (e.g. "SSD"): the question asks for characteristics
"Size" unless it is clearly capacity

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Capacity
2. Access speed

questions.question: Explain **two** drawbacks to the patients of the practice moving appointment booking online.
traps: "to the patients": drawbacks to the practice (cost, training staff) are not credited.
Each drawback needs a consequence for the patient to earn the second mark.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for expanding it (a reason or consequence linked to the scenario), up to 4 marks.
points: Patients without internet access or a suitable device
cannot book online so may have to wait for phone lines / are disadvantaged
Some patients (e.g. elderly) have low IT skills
so they may struggle to use the booking system and book the wrong slot or give up
Less human contact / no one to ask
so patients cannot easily explain urgent dental pain or ask questions while booking
Concerns about personal/medical data being stored online
so patients may worry their details could be leaked or misused
System downtime / website not working
means patients cannot book or change appointments when they need to
reject: Drawbacks to the practice, e.g. set-up cost or staff training
"Hacking" on its own with no link to the patient

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Some elderly patients may not be confident using websites, so they could struggle to book and end up without an appointment.
2. If the booking website goes down, patients cannot book or cancel appointments until it is fixed.

questions.context: The patient records will contain sensitive medical information. Antivirus software will be installed on every computer.
questions.question: Describe how antivirus software protects the patient records stored on the computer system.
traps: Describe how it protects: marks are for the process (scan → compare → quarantine → update), not for saying it "keeps data safe".

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 4 marks.
points: Scans files / emails / downloads / USB devices
Compares files with a database of known malware signatures
Uses heuristic analysis to spot suspicious behaviour / new, unknown malware
Real-time / background monitoring as files are opened
Quarantines or deletes infected files so they cannot damage/encrypt records
Alerts the user when a threat is found
Regularly updates its definitions to detect the latest threats
Scheduled full-system scans
reject: "Stops hackers" (that is a firewall)
"Stops viruses" with no description of how

questions.modelAnswer: Antivirus software scans files, emails and downloads and compares them with a database of known malware signatures. It also uses heuristics to spot suspicious behaviour from new malware. Any infected file is quarantined so it cannot damage the patient records, and the definitions are updated regularly so it can detect the latest threats.

questions.question: Discuss the methods, other than antivirus software and firewalls, the practice could use to protect patient data.
traps: "other than antivirus software and firewalls": any time spent on those two earns nothing.
Discuss means consider both sides, e.g. the benefit of each method and a drawback or limitation.

markScheme.focus: Methods other than antivirus and firewalls, applied to patient data at a dental practice.
indicative: Access levels: receptionists see appointments only; dentists see clinical notes and X-rays
File permissions: read-only vs read/write vs full control, matched to job role
Encryption of stored records so a stolen computer does not expose patient data
Backups (full / incremental / differential) stored off-site or in the cloud, with tested recovery
Physical security: locked server cupboard, keypad on the office door, CCTV
Biometrics or multi-factor authentication for staff logins
Strong password policy / automatic screen lock at reception where patients can see
Staff training so they recognise phishing and do not share passwords
Drawbacks weighed: cost, extra time for staff, training needed
reject: Antivirus software or firewalls (excluded by the question)

questions.modelAnswer:
The practice could set access levels so each member of staff only sees what their job needs. Receptionists would see appointment details, while dentists would also see clinical notes and X-rays. This limits the damage if one account is misused, although it takes time to set up and must be updated when staff change roles.

Patient records should be encrypted. If a laptop or the server was stolen, the data would be unreadable without the key. The drawback is that a lost key could lock the practice out of its own records.

Regular backups, for example a nightly incremental backup and a weekly full backup stored off-site or in the cloud, would let the practice recover records after a fire, failure or ransomware attack. Backups only help if the recovery is tested.

Physical controls matter too: the server should be in a locked room with a keypad, and reception screens should lock automatically because patients stand close to them. Multi-factor authentication would stop a stolen password being enough to log in, but adds a step for busy staff.

questions.context: The app emails a receipt to the customer at the end of each hire.
questions.question: Give **two** protocols used when sending and receiving email.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: SMTP (sending)
POP / POP3 (receiving/downloading)
IMAP (receiving/syncing)
accept: TLS/SSL where linked to securing email
reject: HTTP or HTTPS (web pages, not email protocols)
Email clients such as Outlook

questions.modelAnswer:
1. SMTP
2. IMAP

questions.context: Some head office staff work from home two days a week.
questions.question: Explain **two** benefits to Northway Bikes of staff using a virtual private network (VPN) when working from home.
traps: "to Northway Bikes": explain what the company gains, not what a home user gains from a consumer VPN.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for expanding it (a reason or consequence linked to the scenario), up to 4 marks.
points: Data is sent through an encrypted tunnel
so customer and payment data cannot be read if it is intercepted on a home network
Staff can access internal systems/files as if in the office
so customer support can continue without staff travelling in
Secure use of untrusted networks (home/public Wi-Fi)
reducing the risk of a data breach and fines under data protection law
Only authenticated staff can connect to the company network
so the booking system is protected from unauthorised access
reject: "It is secure" with no explanation
"Hides your IP address/location" (a benefit to an individual, not the company)
Benefits of remote working in general that are not about the VPN

questions.modelAnswer:
1. A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel, so if staff are on insecure home Wi-Fi, customer payment details cannot be read if intercepted.
2. Staff can reach the booking system and shared files as if they were in the office, so customer support keeps running when they work from home.

questions.context: The app updates bike availability at every dock every few seconds.
questions.question: Explain **two** ways high latency could affect customers using the app.
traps: Latency is delay, not the amount of data. Answers about large files downloading slowly describe bandwidth.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for expanding it (a reason or consequence linked to the scenario), up to 4 marks.
points: Bike availability shown is out of date
so a customer may walk to a dock and find no bike available
Delay between scanning the QR code and the bike unlocking
leaving customers waiting at the dock / frustrated
Two customers could book the same bike
because updates reach the server too late, causing booking conflicts
Live map / journey tracking lags behind
so customers see the wrong position or time and are charged incorrectly
reject: A definition of latency on its own
Slow downloads of large files (that is bandwidth, not latency)

questions.modelAnswer:
1. The app would show out-of-date availability, so a customer could arrive at a dock and find the bike already taken.
2. There would be a delay between scanning the QR code and the lock opening, so customers are left waiting at the dock.

questions.context: Every hire records the customer, start and end docks, times, distance and payment.
questions.question: Explain **two** ways Northway Bikes could use the transactional data it collects.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for expanding it (a reason or consequence linked to the scenario), up to 4 marks.
points: Identify the busiest docks and times
so staff can move bikes to where demand is highest / add more docks
Targeted marketing based on journey history
e.g. offering a monthly pass to frequent riders to increase sales
Set prices by demand (peak/off-peak)
to increase revenue at busy times and encourage use when quiet
Plan maintenance from the distance each bike has travelled
so bikes are serviced before they break down
Detect unusual activity / fraud
e.g. many hires from one card in a short time
reject: "To improve the business" with no specific use
Selling customer data (would breach data protection law)

questions.modelAnswer:
1. It can find out which docks are busiest at rush hour, so staff can move bikes there before customers arrive.
2. It can see who hires bikes most often and send them offers for a monthly pass, increasing sales.

questions.question: Evaluate the use of a mobile app, rather than a website, for customers hiring bikes.
traps: "rather than a website": you must compare the two. Listing app features alone stays in the lower levels.
Evaluate needs a judgement at the end that follows from your points.

markScheme.focus: A mobile app compared with a website, for customers hiring bikes, ending with a supported judgement.
indicative: App uses the phone’s GPS to show the nearest docks and route
App uses the camera to scan the QR code and unlock a bike quickly
Push notifications (hire reminders, receipts, offers)
Stored login and payment details make repeat hires quicker
Customer must download and install it, which uses storage and data; one-off tourists may not bother
Separate versions for iOS and Android cost more to build and update
Customers without a smartphone, or with an old one, are excluded
A website works in any browser with no install, but cannot scan a QR code or use GPS as smoothly
Conclusion: app suits regular riders and unlocking; a website is a useful fallback for occasional users

questions.modelAnswer:
A mobile app has clear advantages for hiring bikes. It can use the phone’s GPS to show the nearest dock with a bike available and the camera to scan the QR code, so a customer can unlock a bike in seconds. Login and payment details are stored, so regular commuters can hire again quickly, and push notifications can remind them to return the bike before the price goes up.

However, customers must download and install the app first. A tourist who only wants one ride may give up rather than install it, so Northway could lose one-off hires. Customers without a smartphone, or with an old phone that cannot run the app, are excluded completely. Northway also has to build and update separate iOS and Android versions, which costs more than one website.

A website would work on any device with a browser and needs no installation, which suits occasional users. But it is less convenient at the dock because using the camera and location from a browser is slower and less reliable.

Overall, the app is the better choice because unlocking by QR code and finding bikes by GPS are central to the service, and most customers will be regular riders. Northway should still offer a simple website for booking and support so occasional customers are not lost.

File compression
Disk clean-up
Encryption software
File manager

Operating systems

questions.question: Give **two** assistive technologies the school could provide for a pupil with a visual impairment.
traps: The technology must suit a visual impairment. Eye-tracking is for motor impairments.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each correct answer, up to 2 marks.
points: Screen reader / text-to-speech
Screen magnifier
Braille display / braille embosser
Speech recognition / voice control
High-contrast or large-print keyboard
High-contrast display settings
reject: Technologies for other needs, e.g. eye-tracking or a switch for motor impairments

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Screen reader
2. Screen magnifier

questions.context: The tablets will be shared between classes.
questions.question: Explain **two** factors, other than cost, that affect the school’s choice of operating system for the tablets.
traps: "other than cost": price, licensing and budget answers score nothing.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for expanding it (a reason or consequence linked to the scenario), up to 4 marks.
points: Compatibility with the apps and systems the school already uses
so teachers’ lesson apps and the school network work on the tablets
Security features / frequency of updates
to protect pupil data and keep devices safe from malware
Ease of use / familiar interface
so young pupils and staff need little training
Device management / parental-style controls
so the technician can restrict what pupils install or access
Availability of educational apps
so the tablets support the curriculum
Length of support / update lifespan
so the tablets stay secure for several years
reject: Cost, price or licence fees (excluded by the question)
"It is better" / "It is faster" on its own

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Compatibility: the OS must run the reading and maths apps the school already pays for, or teachers could not use them in lessons.
2. Ease of use: a simple, familiar interface means five-year-olds can use the tablets without lots of help, saving lesson time.

questions.question: Describe **one** type of user interface suitable for pupils aged 5 to 7.
traps: "one": if you describe two, only the first is marked.
The justification must link to the age of the pupils.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for a suitable interface, 1 for a justification, 1 for expanding the justification.
points: Graphical user interface (GUI) with touch input
uses large icons and pictures instead of text, as young pupils cannot read well yet
so they can tap to open apps without needing to use a mouse or type
Speech / voice interface
pupils can speak commands instead of reading or typing
which suits children whose reading and spelling are still developing
Menu-driven interface
offers a small number of choices on screen
so pupils cannot get lost or change settings by mistake
reject: Command-line interface (needs typed commands)
More than one interface: only the first is marked

questions.modelAnswer: A touch-screen GUI would suit them because it uses large icons and pictures rather than text, which matters because many pupils this age cannot read well. They can simply tap an icon to open an app, so they do not need mouse skills.

questions.context: The school plans to set homework on an online learning platform that pupils access from home.
questions.question: Evaluate the moral and ethical implications of setting homework on an online learning platform.
traps: Moral and ethical means fairness, privacy, accessibility and wellbeing, not the school’s costs.
A conclusion that simply says "it is good" without conditions will not reach Level 3.

markScheme.focus: Moral and ethical implications for pupils and families of online homework, weighed up with a conclusion.
indicative: Digital divide: some families have no device, only a shared phone, or no broadband
Pupils with disabilities need the platform to work with assistive technology
Privacy: pupil data (names, work, progress) held by a third-party provider; consent from parents
Online safety: messaging features could allow contact from strangers or cyberbullying
Health: more screen time for young children
Positives: resources available at any time, instant feedback, adaptive tasks, parents can see progress
Environment: less paper, but more devices and energy use
Mitigations: loan devices, paper alternative, homework club, GDPR-compliant provider
Conclusion: acceptable only if the school provides alternatives so no pupil is disadvantaged

questions.modelAnswer:
Online homework has real benefits. Pupils can access resources at any time, get instant feedback on their answers, and parents can log in to see their child’s progress. Tasks can adapt to each pupil’s level, which helps those who are struggling as well as those who need a challenge.

The main ethical concern is fairness. Some families have no computer, share one phone between several children, or have no broadband. Those pupils would be unable to complete homework through no fault of their own, which widens the gap between them and their classmates. Pupils with visual or motor impairments may also be excluded if the platform does not work with screen readers or other assistive technology.

There are privacy issues too. The platform would hold pupils’ names, work and progress data on a third party’s servers, so the school must make sure the provider complies with data protection law and that parents understand what is collected. If the platform has messaging, young children could be exposed to cyberbullying or contact from strangers.

Overall, online homework is ethically acceptable only if the school removes the barriers. It should lend devices or run a homework club, offer a paper alternative, and choose an accessible, GDPR-compliant platform with messaging turned off. Without these steps, the benefits would go mainly to pupils who are already advantaged.

questions.question:
Draw a diagram to show how the office network is set up and how architects connect when on site visits.

The diagram must include:
• devices and systems that are used
• connection types and annotations.
traps: Every room in the stem is a mark: miss a room and you lose a mark.
"connection types and annotations": unlabelled lines earn nothing.
Draw it on paper, then tick what your diagram shows.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for each feature shown correctly, up to 6 marks.
points: Design studio: six desktops AND the printer connected to a switch (wired, e.g. Ethernet)
Meeting room: smart TV connected through a wireless access point (Wi-Fi)
Server cupboard: file server connected to the switch
Router connected to the internet, with a firewall between the internet and the office network
Tablet connects over a mobile network (4G/5G / cell tower) to the internet, then to the server (e.g. via VPN)
Complete, working system with every device and connection type labelled
accept: Wired or wireless connections, as long as they are labelled and sensible
reject: Devices not in the scenario
Unlabelled lines (no connection type)
Tablet connected directly to the server with no internet link

questions.modelAnswer: Studio PCs ×6 and printer → switch (Ethernet). Switch → file server (Ethernet). Switch → router → firewall → internet. Wireless access point on the switch → smart TV (Wi-Fi). Tablet → 4G/5G cell tower → internet → firewall → file server (VPN, encrypted). Every line labelled with its connection type.

questions.question: Explain **one** factor that affects the choice of connection type for the computers in the design studio.
traps: "one": only your first factor is marked.
"Faster" on its own earns nothing. Say what is faster and why it matters here.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for a factor, 1 for an expansion linked to the design studio.
points: Bandwidth / transfer speed
drawings are large files, so a wired Gigabit Ethernet connection transfers them quickly
Reliability / interference
a wired connection is not affected by walls or other devices, so it will not drop while saving work
Security
cables are harder to intercept than Wi-Fi, protecting client designs
Mobility
the desktops do not move, so the flexibility of wireless is not needed
Cost of installation
running cables to six desks costs more than one access point
reject: "Faster" or "better" with no reason
Compatibility

questions.modelAnswer: Bandwidth: the architects save very large drawing files, so a wired Ethernet connection is needed to transfer them to the file server quickly.

questions.context: Clients often complain that emailed drawings take a long time to arrive.
questions.question: Explain **two** ways the firm could reduce the time taken to send drawings to clients.
traps: Lossy compression is wrong for technical drawings because detail would be lost.

markScheme.rule: 1 mark for identifying a point and 1 more for expanding it (a reason or consequence linked to the scenario), up to 4 marks.
points: Compress files using lossless compression (e.g. ZIP)
makes files smaller to send without losing any detail from the drawing
Convert to a suitable file format (e.g. PDF instead of the original CAD file)
which is smaller and opens on any device
Share a cloud link instead of an email attachment
the client downloads only when needed and attachment size limits are avoided
Upgrade the internet connection / increase bandwidth
so more data is sent per second
reject: Lossy compression (would lose detail from technical drawings)
"Use a faster computer" (not about transmission)

questions.modelAnswer:
1. Compress the drawings with lossless compression such as ZIP. The files become smaller so they send faster, and no detail in the drawing is lost.
2. Send a PDF instead of the original design file. It is much smaller and the client can open it without special software.

questions.question: Evaluate the suitability of cloud storage, compared to the on-site file server, for storing the firm’s drawings.
traps: "compared to": every point should say how cloud is better or worse than the server they already have.
12 marks: you need depth on both sides (performance AND suitability) and a conclusion that follows from them.

markScheme.focus: Cloud storage against the existing on-site server for large drawing files, both used at the office and on site, ending with a judgement.
indicative: Cloud: architects can open drawings on site over 4G/5G without needing a VPN into the office
Cloud: provider handles backup and disaster recovery; a fire at the office would not destroy the drawings
Cloud: scalable storage, pay per month rather than buying and replacing server hardware
Cloud: easier to share with clients using links / collaborate
Cloud: large files must upload/download over the internet, slower than the office LAN; slow sites suffer
Cloud: no access at all if the internet fails; ongoing subscription cost

The cloud provider would also handle backups and disaster recovery. If the office had a fire or the server failed, the drawings would still be safe. Storage can be increased as the firm grows, and the monthly subscription replaces the cost of buying and maintaining a server.

Performance is the main weakness. Drawings are very large, and opening or saving them over the internet is much slower than over the office LAN. questions.modelAnswer:
The Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR give members strong protection. The society must keep data secure and accurate and use it only for the purpose it was collected. Members have the right to see what is held about them and to have errors corrected. Because a serious breach can lead to large fines from the ICO and must be reported, the society has a strong incentive to invest in security and train its staff.

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access to computer systems, and changing data without permission, criminal offences. This deters hackers and gives the police powers to prosecute them.

However, the laws have clear limits. They mostly act after harm has been done. A fine does not return a member’s stolen savings or undo identity theft. markScheme.focus: Learners evaluate the features of utility software that can be used to maintain, manage and optimise the computer system.
indicative: File management: organise files and folders by creating, copying, moving, renaming and deleting
Antivirus: real-time protection, scheduled background scans, quarantines or removes infected files, heuristic analysis for new threats, automatic definition updates
Disk defragmenter: rearranges fragmented files so data is stored contiguously, cutting access, boot and load times; consolidates free space
Backup and recovery: scheduled full / incremental / differential backups, multiple versions kept, encrypted, quick restore if the OS fails
File compression: files take less disk space and upload / download faster; can be compressed and encrypted together
Disk cleanup: deletes temporary files, cache, cookies and history so boot and load times improve; runs on a schedule; makes restore points first
Firewall: monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic against rules; rules and threat databases update automatically
Password manager: generates unique encrypted passwords; flags weak, reused, old or compromised passwords
Encryption software: makes data unreadable to unauthorised users; authenticates users and devices; detects unauthorised changes
Conclusion: utility software improves the performance, security and efficiency of the system and keeps it reliable and easy to use

questions.modelAnswer:
Defragmenter: reorders fragmented files so booking records load faster, but it does little for SSDs.
Antivirus: scheduled scans and real-time protection quarantine malware before it corrupts customer data, but it needs constant updates and can slow the PC during scans.
Backup utility: scheduled incremental backups keep every branch's data recoverable, but they need storage and testing.
Disk cleanup: removes temporary files to free space and speed up start-up, though the gain is small on a well-kept system.
Conclusion: antivirus and backup matter most because they protect customer data; defrag and cleanup help, but less.

indicative: Consent: failing to get clients' consent to store their data damages trust and reputation; clients have the right to know what is collected and to control how it is used

Secure storage prevents breaches and penalties under the Data Protection Act; poor security risks theft or misuse, upset clients and damage to the company's image, making it harder to attract customers, investors and partners

which is dedicated to one organisation

Public cloud

and set up and managed by a third-party service provider

questions.question: Evaluate how different cloud computing models could fit the needs of Just U Games.
traps: Cloud computing MODELS: deployment (public, private, hybrid) and / or service (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), each judged against Just U Games' needs.

markScheme.focus: Learners evaluate how different cloud computing models fit the needs of Just U Games.
indicative: IaaS: servers, storage and networking the company configures itself; full control and high performance without buying expensive hardware; scales up or down quickly
IaaS: suits hosting multiplayer games, with powerful virtual machines (CPUs / GPUs) maintained by the provider
PaaS: the provider manages the environment; built-in tools speed up development and updates; scales with player numbers; less control and customisation

SaaS: lower upfront costs and subscription pricing; ready-made software maintained by the vendor; analytics on player retention and behaviour; limited customisation, and player data held on third-party servers
SaaS: the provider supplies security and backup: encryption, disaster recovery, automatic backup and DDoS protection
Private cloud: self-hosted or dedicated; full control over performance, data and costs; lower latency and stronger security for player data and payments
Public cloud: pay only for the resources used; add or remove servers with demand; global reach; provider handles DDoS protection, backup and recovery
Hybrid cloud: in-house infrastructure plus rented cloud capacity when needed; flexible and reliable, keeps sensitive data in-house, but more complex to manage and needs networking expertise
Conclusion: each model offers different control, flexibility, cost and responsibility; Just U Games should choose on scalability, security, performance and budget

questions.modelAnswer:
Public cloud: cheap pay-as-you-go storage that scales as the player base grows, but player data sits on a third party's servers.
Private cloud: full control and stronger security for accounts and payments, but expensive to build and run.
Hybrid: passwords and payment data stay private while bulk game data backs up to the public cloud; flexible, but harder to manage.
IaaS: rents servers and storage on demand, good for backup and scaling, but the company still configures and secures them.
Conclusion: hybrid fits best, cheap scalable backup for bulk data with sensitive player data kept private.

questions.context: Just U Games uses a file server to store gaming data and is considering installing a web server to host games.
questions.question: Evaluate the performance and efficiency of a web server compared to a file server to support online multiplayer gaming.
traps: Compare BOTH servers on performance AND efficiency for live multiplayer, then conclude.
"Use both" only works if you say what each one is for: file server for downloads, web server for live play.

markScheme.focus: Learners evaluate performance and efficiency of a web server compared to a file server to support online multiplayer gaming.
indicative: Web server: handles HTTP requests, session management and game back-end services; optimised for many small requests at once
Web server: low latency, continuous state updates and two-way communication (HTTP/2, WebSockets); event-driven, so it handles thousands or millions of connections
Web server: resource efficient, with efficient memory per connection and small, frequent packets; near-instant responses for movement, chat and synchronisation
Web server: easily scalable; REST APIs or sockets keep gaming sessions reliable; outperforms a file server for real-time play
File server: stores and delivers static files (game assets, downloads, updates, patches); optimised for large file throughput and sequential reads / writes
File server: high latency for frequent small reads / writes; inefficient for small real-time packets because of connection setup and input / output waits
File server: concurrency limited by input / output and locks; requests queue; needs heavy caching; no live updates
File server: harder to scale globally because it is storage-bound; reliability focuses on file integrity; unsuitable for live multiplayer

Conclusion: a web server is much better for multiplayer (real-time communication, low latency, many players, synchronisation); a file server suits storing and sharing files, backups and asset downloads

questions.modelAnswer:
Web server: built for many small, frequent requests, so player moves and chat update with low latency; event-driven, so thousands of players connect at once.
File server: built for large transfers, so it delivers downloads and patches efficiently, but small real-time updates queue behind input / output waits and add lag.
Scalability: web servers spread across regions; a file server is storage-bound and harder to scale.
Conclusion: host live games on the web server and keep the file server for assets and updates.

Format check: e.g. postcode or phone number must match a pattern; stops badly typed contact details

Presence check: owner phone numbers cannot be left blank, so the clinic can always call; but a mistyped number still passes.

questions.question: Evaluate the suitability of a star topology and a bus topology for the depot's network.

markScheme.focus: The suitability of star and bus topologies for a busy depot network.
indicative: Star: every device has its own cable to a central switch; the most common topology
Star: easy to add devices and find faults; one cable failing only affects one device
Star: the switch is a single point of failure; uses more cable, so costs more to install
Bus: all devices share one backbone cable; cheap, with minimal cabling
Bus: only one device can transmit at a time, so it slows down as devices are added
Bus: a break in the backbone takes the whole network down; needs terminators at each end
Depot needs: many scanners and PCs, busy periods, growth, and little tolerance for downtime
Conclusion: star suits the depot because it handles many devices and isolates faults, despite the higher cabling cost

questions.modelAnswer:
Star: each PC has its own cable to a switch, so one broken cable stops one device, not the depot; but the switch is a single point of failure and more cable costs more.
Bus: one shared backbone is cheap to install; but only one device can send at a time, so it slows as scanners are added, and one break stops everything.
The depot runs many devices at busy times and cannot afford downtime.
Conclusion: star is more suitable; the extra cabling cost is worth the reliability.

questions.question: Evaluate how the features and components of the venue's network affect performance during a live tournament.
